title: The bent-over woman (Luke 13:10–17)
hookLine: eighteen years stooped; he calls her a daughter of Abraham and she stands up straight

lines: EIGHTEEN YEARS LOOKING AT THE GROUND.
cards: Eighteen years. That is how long, Luke says, this woman has been bent over, looking at the ground: feet, dust, the hems of other people's clothes. She can't look up to see a face or the sky.

Luke, who tradition says was a physician, describes her carefully: she "was bowed together, and could in no wise lift up herself." On a Sabbath she does what she has probably done for years. She comes to the synagogue.
Nobody says she asked for anything. Jesus is teaching, and he sees her.

teach.b: He calls her over: "Woman, thou art loosed from thine infirmity." He lays his hands on her, "and immediately she was made straight, and glorified God."
After eighteen years, perhaps the first thing she sees, looking up, is his face. Then comes an objection worth hearing fairly.

teach.h: SIX DAYS FOR HEALING, HE SAYS.
teach.b: The leader of the synagogue is indignant and tells the crowd: "There are six days in which men ought to work: in them therefore come and be healed, and not on the sabbath day."

He's protecting something precious, the Sabbath rest God commanded. He isn't against healing; he's against doing it today. Jesus answers with an argument the leader would recognize, from the lesser to the greater.
On the Sabbath, every one of you unties your ox or donkey and leads it to water.
Then: "And ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan hath bound, lo, these eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?"

teach.h: UNTIE THE OX; LOOSE THE WOMAN.
teach.b: In Luke's Greek, untie and loose are the same verb, and bound is its opposite. If an animal can be untied for a drink, how much more a woman bound for eighteen years?
And notice the title: daughter of Abraham. For eighteen years she had been the bent woman, a body people stepped around.

teach.h: SHE WAS MADE STRAIGHT, AND GLORIFIED GOD.
teach.b: He gives her a family name, a place in Israel's story. Luke says all the people rejoiced. The Sabbath, a day of freedom, became the day she was set free.

how: Some churches pray for the sick with the laying on of hands, as Jesus does here, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians also anoint the sick with oil.

o: Israel's forefather, giving her a family name
a prophet who healed on the Sabbath long ago
the synagogue leader who objected that day

games.q: what's inside Luke 13:10–17 — tap the pairs.
p: six days to come and be healed
a family name in Israel's story

s: the woman asked Jesus to heal her
Luke says nothing of her asking. Jesus sees her and calls her over.
Jesus argues from the leader's own practice of untying animals on the Sabbath
if an ox can be untied for a drink, how much more a woman bound eighteen years.
the synagogue leader objects to healing altogether
he says come on the other six days, and not on the Sabbath.

games.q: you're the synagogue leader. a woman has just been healed on the Sabbath, in your synagogue. what do you say to the crowd?
o: there are six days to work: come and be healed then.
this teacher must leave at once.
games.why: "there are six days in which men ought to work: in them therefore come and be healed." Jesus answers with the ox untied for water.

practice: Stand if you can, or sit forward, and let your head drop toward your chest; notice how small the world gets.
Then roll slowly upward, one bone at a time, until your eyes find the room, and breathe at your full height, thinking of whatever has kept you bent lately: a weight, a worry, someone's words.
If you pray, hear the words thou art loosed; if you don't, simply stand in your own height.

wordCard.voice: Abraham. Jesus calls the bent-over woman a daughter of Abraham as he heals her, giving her a family name and a place in Israel's story.

orig.note: Greek: you have been set free, loosed. the same root runs through untie the ox and loose the woman.

carryVoice: Your line: daughter, you are loosed. Eighteen years ended with a touch. Day five hundred fifty-two.
